A USD investment needs a dated CAD cost record: convert the purchase and sale separately

Four editable graphics reconcile separately translated cost and proceeds, explain the price/currency decomposition and stress a CAD result even when the USD difference is zero.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Keep acquisition-date cost and disposition-date proceeds in their own CAD conversions

Interactive planning lab

CAD arithmetic gain or loss before inclusion$3,650
Historical CAD acquisition cost$12,500
CAD translation of gross disposition proceeds$16,200

Original hypothetical USD capital-property example for one purchase, no later adjusted-cost changes and a full disposition. Acquisition cost is translated at its independently entered acquisition-date CAD-per-USD rate; gross disposition proceeds use the disposition-date rate. Eligible disposition expenses are supplied already in CAD and subtracted once. No quoted market rates are imported. All chart results are CAD arithmetic before an inclusion rate, tax, loss-eligibility rules or other income. No actual currency conversion, settlement receipt, spending cash, later disposition of USD cash, pooled-cost calculation, partial sale, reinvestment, dividend or registered-account treatment is modeled. A negative result is an arithmetic loss, not a determination that it may be claimed.

The central idea

A CAD capital-property calculation needs dated CAD proceeds, cost and expenses. A USD profit translated at one rate can omit the currency change on the original cost.

01

Give the cost and proceeds separate conversion dates

A USD statement can show a clear profit while leaving a Canadian-dollar record incomplete. The amount paid, the sale proceeds and the relevant expenses need compatible units before they can be reconciled.

CRA’s capital-gains guidance says to convert foreign-currency proceeds using the rate at sale, the adjusted cost base using the rate at acquisition, and disposition expenses using the rate when incurred.

This article isolates one purchase followed by a full disposition, with no later adjusted-cost changes. The acquisition input includes any eligible costs incurred on that same purchase date. Disposition expenses are entered separately after conversion to CAD. The example does not rebuild a pooled cost base from several purchases or later adjustments.

All rates here are invented. The Bank of Canada’s rate page expresses its foreign quotes as one unit of foreign currency converted into CAD and describes them as indicative averages. The tool uses that clearly stated quote direction without importing a current quote or assuming a bank would execute at an indicative rate.

02

Reconcile a single-purchase example in CAD

The authored example starts with USD 10,000 of acquisition cost and an acquisition-date rate of CAD 1.25 for USD 1. That produces a historical CAD cost of 10,000 × 1.25, or CAD 12,500.

The full disposition has USD 12,000 of gross proceeds. Its separately entered sale-date rate is CAD 1.35 for USD 1, producing CAD 16,200 of translated proceeds. Eligible disposition expenses have already been converted and are entered as CAD 50.

The first waterfall therefore computes CAD 16,200 minus CAD 12,500 minus CAD 50, giving a CAD 3,650 arithmetic gain before any inclusion rate or personal tax calculation.

Each number has its own role. The acquisition amount is a historical cost record, the translated proceeds describe the disposition value, and the expense reduces the result once. The three headline metrics should not be added together as household assets.

03

Explain the currency effect on the original cost

The USD change in this example is 12,000 minus 10,000, or USD 2,000. Translating only that difference at the sale rate gives CAD 2,700 before the CAD expense. It leaves another part of the dated CAD reconciliation unexplained.

The original USD 10,000 cost is affected by the change between the two rates. Multiplying it by 1.35 minus 1.25 gives CAD 1,000. The second waterfall adds CAD 2,700 and CAD 1,000, then subtracts the CAD 50 expense, reaching the same CAD 3,650 result.

That is one exact algebraic decomposition. The USD-change term is translated at the full sale rate, so it already incorporates the interaction between the USD change and the currency movement. Adding another interaction amount would count part of the result twice.

The decomposition explains the record. It does not identify two separate deposits, attribute a trading skill or calculate the payoff from an actual currency hedge.

04

Zero USD difference does not require zero CAD difference

Set USD gross proceeds equal to the original USD 10,000 acquisition cost, while keeping the default acquisition rate, sale rate and CAD expense. The USD difference becomes zero.

The translated CAD proceeds are now CAD 13,500. Historical CAD cost remains CAD 12,500. After the CAD 50 expense, the arithmetic CAD gain is CAD 950. No USD price profit is needed for that result.

The signed bars keep the equal-USD condition and vary the sale rate. At a rate of CAD 1.00 per USD, the arithmetic result is negative CAD 2,550. At the acquisition rate of 1.25, only the CAD 50 expense remains as a negative result. At a sale rate of 1.50, the arithmetic gain is CAD 2,450.

These are separate stress cases. A negative value is not automatically an eligible capital loss, and the chart does not test restrictions, other transactions or special property rules. It also assigns no probability to any currency path.

05

Keep a tax record and a bank-cash plan on their own bases

The matrix changes gross USD proceeds and the sale-date rate together. Its column labels are USD amounts, its row labels are CAD-per-USD rates, and its cell values are CAD arithmetic results. The original purchase-date cost remains fixed.

A CAD translation used to prepare a record is not proof that the sale proceeds were exchanged into CAD. If settlement produces USD cash that is retained, a later exchange or disposition of that cash creates another record question outside this model. Conversion spreads, actual bank receipts and spending dates require their own ledger.

The calculator also stops before tax. It uses no inclusion rate, tax bracket, loss deduction, foreign tax credit or refund estimate. A registered-account transaction, income-account treatment, several acquisition dates, reinvestment or later ACB adjustments would require a different scope.

Retain the purchase evidence, its CAD conversion, any subsequent cost adjustments, the sale evidence and separately converted expenses. A single current exchange rate cannot reconstruct that history from a USD statement’s net profit alone.

The CRA page reviewed on 25 October 2026 contains 2025-return material. Its conversion framework supports this limited educational example; the tool does not prepare a return or determine the treatment of a proposed transaction.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All USD amounts, CAD expenses and CAD-per-USD rates are original hypothetical inputs for one purchase and full disposition with no later cost adjustments. The charts calculate arithmetic before inclusion and personal tax, not claimable loss eligibility or bank cash. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
